content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review:
Summary:

To utilize the hierarchical label structures, this paper proposed Hierarchical Complement Objective Training (HCOT) which regularizes the entropy of the posterior distribution over the rest of classes (all classes except ground truth class) based on the label hierarchies. The authors showed that the proposed method can be useful for image classification and segmentation tasks. 

Detailed comments:

Even though the proposed method improves the performances on image classification and segmentation tasks, the proposed idea looks like a simple variant of existing work [Chen' 19]. Because of that, it is hard to evaluate the novelty of this paper. Also, there are many papers [Bilal' 17, Goo' 16, Xie' 15, Jiang' 17] to utilize the label hierarchies for various purposes in the literature, but the authors did not compare the proposed method with them. 

Minor comments:

- In equation (5), is there no hyper-parameter to balance the XE and HCE?

- I think it would be interesting if the authors can consider a case with (partial) hierarchical label structures. 

[Chen' 19] Hao-Yun Chen, Pei-Hsin Wang, Chun-Hao Liu, Shih-Chieh Chang, Jia-Yu Pan, Yu-Ting Chen, Wei Wei, and Da-Cheng Juan. Complement objective training. In ICLR 2019.

[Bilal' 17] Bilal, A., Jourabloo, A., Ye, M., Liu, X. and Ren, L., 2017. Do convolutional neural networks learn class hierarchy?. IEEE transactions on visualization and computer graphics, 24(1), pp.152-162.

[Goo' 16] Goo, W., Kim, J., Kim, G. and Hwang, S.J., 2016, October. Taxonomy-regularized semantic deep convolutional neural networks. In European Conference on Computer Vision (pp. 86-101). Springer, Cham.

[Xie' 15] Xie, S., Yang, T., Wang, X. and Lin, Y., 2015. Hyper-class augmented and regularized deep learning for fine-grained image classification. In Proceedings of the IEEE conference on computer vision and pattern recognition (pp. 2645-2654).

[Jiang' 17] Jiang, Y.G., Wu, Z., Wang, J., Xue, X. and Chang, S.F., 2017. Exploiting feature and class relationships in video categorization with regularized deep neural networks. IEEE transactions on pattern analysis and machine intelligence, 40(2), pp.352-364.

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer #1
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the detailed reviews and constructive feedback.

(Q1) The proposed idea looks like a simple variant of existing work [Chen' 19].

(A1) The existing work “COT” [Chen' 19] cannot leverage the information from label hierarchy for training, whereas the proposed HCOT effectively uses the label hierarchy to improve the performance of various tasks.


(Q2) Authors did not compare the proposed method with some related works.
 
(A2) We thank the reviewer for providing several works on utilizing the label hierarchies. We conducted an additional experiment to compare the proposed method and one previous work (suggested by the reviewer) that focuses on the image classification (CNN-RNN). The experimental results are provided in the table R1 below. Compared to this previous work, experimental results show HCOT is able to utilize the label hierarchies more effectively. As for the rest of the suggested previous works, those are focused on different domains (e.g., videos) and therefore are not directly comparable with the tasks considered in this paper. Nevertheless, we will cite these works in the manuscript to make the related works more comprehensive. 

Table R1. Classification results (accuracy%) of models trained with CNN-RNN and HCOT on CIFAR100
===========================================================
Method            WRN-28-10     Wider-ResNet
CNN-RNN 	76.23                79.14
HCOT             79.68                79.75 
===========================================================


For your minor comments:

(Q1) In equation (5), is there no hyper-parameter to balance the XE and HCE?

(A1) There is no hyper-parameter existed to balance the XE and HCE, since treating them “equal weight” works very well already and the additional hyperparameter is not necessary.


(Q2)  I think it would be interesting if the authors can consider a case with (partial) hierarchical label structures. 

(A2) Thanks for the interesting suggestion. As suggested, we conducted an additional experiment on partial hierarchical label structures; we randomly select 50% label hierarchies out of CIFAR-100 dataset and train the model with HCOT. The experimental results are provided in the table R2 below. Notice that HCOT still achieves good improvement compared to COT in image classification task. Yet, the improvement is not as significant due to part of the hierarchical label information is missing.

Table R2. Error rates (%) on CIFAR-100 using ResNet.
===========================================================
Model              Baseline     COT       Partial-Hierarchy COT   HCOT
ResNet-56 	 29.41           27.76     27.55                                27.3
ResNet-110     27.93          27.24     26.97                                26.46

===========================================================


Reference:

[Chen' 19] Hao-Yun Chen, Pei-Hsin Wang, Chun-Hao Liu, Shih-Chieh Chang, Jia-Yu Pan, Yu-Ting Chen, Wei Wei, and Da-Cheng Juan. Complement objective training. In ICLR 2019.

[Guo’ 18] CNN-RNN: a large-scale hierarchical image classification framework.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
1 For the segmentation experiments, the authors only compare HCOT with COT. We can’t know whether adopting the hierarchical mechanism will improve the segmentation performance or not.
 
2 For the image classification experiments, the authors only evaluated the situation of two levels of labels. What is the performance of more than two levels? 
 
3 It seems like there are no validation datasets in the experiments. It is not clear whether they are overfitting or not. 
 
4 In the real-world, the classes often have tree-like hierarchies. This manuscript did not consider this situation. There are also no experiments in dealing with the tree-like label hierarchy.
 
5 Training by alternating optimization (apply twice loss update from both cross-entropy and complement loss) doubles training steps. Not quite a fair comparison (not sure / also not explained).
 
6 Not supporting details on why one method is better than the other in specific cases. Lack of insight into why it is better than the state of the art.

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer #2
content.comment:
Thanks for the constructive comments. Please see our replies below:


(Q1) For the segmentation experiments, the authors only compare HCOT with COT. We can’t know whether adopting the hierarchical mechanism will improve the segmentation performance or not.

(A1) We believe the reviewer wants to see the comparison between “baseline”, “model trained with COT” and “model trained with HCOT”, since in the paper the comparison between “baseline” and “model trained with HCOT” has already been provided. To make sure the improvement on the segmentation from HCOT comes from leveraging the label hierarchy, we have conducted the experiment and performed a three-way comparison in the table below. Note that “segmentation models trained with COT”  (complement without considering label hierarchies) did not achieve significant improvement on both PixAcc and MIoU. We will add this result in Table 6(b) in the final version of the manuscript.

Table 6(b). Segmentation results of “EncNet+JPU” models trained with cross-entropy (denoted as XE) versus COT and HCOT on PASCAL-Context dataset.
===========================================================
		PixAcc    MIoU%
XE 		0.7880    51.05 
COT         0.7884    51.07
HCOT      0.7918    51.35     
===========================================================


(Q2 & Q4) For the image classification experiments, the authors only evaluated the situation of two levels of labels. What is the performance of more than two levels? In the real-world, the classes often have tree-like hierarchies. This manuscript did not consider this situation. There are also no experiments in dealing with the tree-like label hierarchy.

(A2 & A4) To cope with tree-like hierarchies datasets in the real-world (e.g. ImageNet we mentioned in Section 4.2), we follow the state-of-the-art paper working on semantic segmentation: YOLO9000 [Redmon’ 17] to take proper synsets as our coarse label candidates and group fine classes which belong to the same subtree to build two-level hierarchies between synsets and fine classes. As a matter of fact, many literature [Ristin ‘15, Guo’ 18] that aims at improving imagenet classification use similar preprocess steps to turn a tree based hierarchy into two-level hierarchy.  


(Q3) It seems like there are no validation datasets in the experiments. It is not clear whether they are overfitting or not. 

(A3) There are two reasons here: (1) CIFAR100 do not officially provide validation set, and there is no way that we can report results on such a dataset. (2) Although we don't have a dev set, testing dataset can already serve as an evaluation on the generality of HCOT. 


(Q5) Training by alternating optimization (apply twice loss update from both cross-entropy and complement loss) doubles training steps. Not quite a fair comparison (not sure / also not explained).

(A5) In table R1, we conducted only “the primary objective with double training steps” to have a fair comparison with “alternatively using primary and complement objective” and the experimental results show that all the improvements in HCOT are result of the concept of complement but not more training steps.

Table R1. Classification results (accuracy%) of ResNet trained with “double step XE(primary objective)” and “alternatively using XE and HCOT(complement objective)” on CIFAR100.
===========================================================
Model              Double step XE              Alternatively using XE and HCOT
ResNet-56 	  29.28                               27.3
ResNet-110     27.61                               26.46
===========================================================


(Q6) Not supporting details on why one method is better than the other in specific cases. Lack of insight into why it is better than the state of the art.

(A6) The proposed HCOT can further penalize the distribution of the incorrect classes in hierarchy fashion, which lead models to have better generalization to real-world dataset. We argue that this is a strong insight to explain why the state-of-the-art model trained with HCOT can always have significant improvement on classification and segmentation.


Reference:

[Redmon’ 17]. Yolo9000: Better, faster, stronger. In CVPR’17

[Ristin ‘15]. From Categories to Subcategories: Large-scale Image Classification with Partial Class Label Refinement. In CVPR’15

[Guo’ 18] CNN-RNN: a large-scale hierarchical image classification framework.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review:
While the general direction of this work is nice it is unfortunate that the authors did not compare to the many related approaches. 
It is unclear how the approach would be used for tree structures like wordnet and imagenet. 

Unclear novelty due to lack of comparisons to many very related approaches.
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer #3
content.comment:
Thanks for your appreciation in our general direction.

(1.) For the comparison to the state-of-the-art related work focusing on improving image classification using label hierarchies, we have done in the rebuttal of Reviewer #2, please check it out and we can have further discussions.

(2.) To cope with general tree-like hierarchies cases, we follow the related approaches working on utilizing the label hierarchies on ImageNet-2012 to turn tree-like hierarchies into two-level hierarchies and then we can still use HCOT to leverage the information from them. For the details, please check the rebuttal to Reviewer #2.
